category.name: Developer & CI/CD
category.description: Leaked secrets, compromised build systems, tampered pipelines, source control abuse, and developer tooling incidents.

playbooks.name: Secret committed to a public repository
playbooks.summary: Use when an API key, cloud credential, or password is pushed to a public GitHub or GitLab repository, where automated scrapers can harvest it within minutes of the push.

preparation: Enable secret scanning and push protection on all public repositories
Register with providers' partner programs so leaked tokens are auto-revoked and reported
Keep a runbook mapping each secret type to its revocation console
identification: Identify the secret type, owning service, and the commit SHA and time it was pushed
Check whether the repository was public at push time and for how long
Search the secret's provider audit logs for use since the push timestamp
Check for forks or mirrors of the repository that retain the commit
containment: Revoke or rotate the exposed secret at the provider immediately
Block source IPs that used the secret after the leak
Temporarily make the repository private if more secrets may be present
eradication: Rewrite history to remove the secret and request a cache purge from the hosting provider
Ask the hosting provider to remove forks that still contain the commit
Undo any resources or changes the attacker made using the secret
recovery: Deploy the replacement secret through the secrets manager rather than config files
Confirm dependent services work with the new secret
Monitor the old secret identifier for further attempted use
lessons: Measure time from push to revocation
Review why push protection did not block the commit
Add pre-commit secret scanning to developer tooling

splunk.title: Secret scanning alerts and push protection bypasses
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action IN ("secret_scanning_alert.create","secret_scanning_push_protection.bypass","repo.access") repo="<org>/<repo>" | table _time actor action repo

splunk.title: Use of leaked AWS key after push
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.accessKeyId="<leaked_key_id>" earliest=<push_time> | stats count values(eventName) as events by sourceIPAddress userAgent | sort - count

playbooks.name: Long-lived secret found in private repository history
playbooks.summary: Use when a scan or code review finds credentials buried in old commits of an internal repository, readable by every employee, contractor, and integration with repo access.

preparation: Run scheduled full-history secret scans over all internal repositories
Track who and which apps have read access to each repository
Keep repository clone and download audit events in the SIEM
identification: Determine when the secret was committed and whether it is still valid
List all users, deploy keys, and apps that had read access since the commit
Review repository clone and archive download events for unusual accessors
Check the secret's target system logs for use from non-production sources
containment: Rotate the secret and update consuming services via the secrets manager
Remove stale collaborators and unused app installations from the repository
Restrict the repository to the owning team while cleanup proceeds
eradication: Purge the secret from history with git filter-repo and force-push all branches
Ask team members to delete local clones containing the old history
Scan related repositories for the same secret value
recovery: Re-open repository access to the original audience after cleanup
Verify the scanner no longer reports the secret in any branch or tag
Document the rotation in the asset's credential record
lessons: Measure how long the secret sat in history before detection
Add rotation age policies for credentials of this type
Review whether the service could use workload identity instead of a static secret

splunk.title: Clones and archive downloads of the repository
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action IN ("git.clone","repo.download_zip","git.fetch") repo="<org>/<repo>" | stats count min(_time) as first by actor actor_ip | convert ctime(first) | sort - count

splunk.title: Authentication with the leaked service credential
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.user="<service_account>" by Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.action | sort - count

playbooks.name: CI/CD build runner compromised
playbooks.summary: Use when a shared build agent or runner shows signs of attacker control, such as unknown processes, outbound connections, or tampered toolchains, putting every build and secret it handles at risk.

preparation: Use ephemeral runners that are destroyed after each job where possible
Send runner host process and network telemetry to the SIEM
Document which pipelines and secrets each runner pool serves
identification: Capture memory and disk of the suspect runner before it is recycled
List jobs that executed on the runner since the earliest suspicious activity
Review outbound connections from the runner to destinations outside package mirrors
Compare compilers, build tools, and caches on the runner against the golden image
containment: Remove the runner from its pool and block its network egress
Rotate all secrets injected into jobs that ran on the runner
Pause release pipelines that used the runner pool
eradication: Destroy the runner and rebuild the pool from a verified image
Invalidate shared build caches populated by the compromised runner
Identify and close the initial access path, such as an exposed agent API
recovery: Rebuild and re-sign artifacts produced by the runner in the compromise window
Compare rebuilt artifacts against released ones to detect tampering
Resume pipelines on the rebuilt pool with heightened monitoring
lessons: Move remaining persistent runners to ephemeral instances
Add alerting on runner egress outside approved destinations
Measure how many releases were built on the compromised runner

splunk.title: Unusual processes on runner hosts
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.dest IN ("<runner_host>") NOT Processes.parent_process_name IN ("Runner.Worker","gitlab-runner","java") by Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.user

splunk.title: Runner egress to non-approved destinations
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src="<runner_ip>" NOT All_Traffic.dest IN (<approved_mirrors>) by All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port | sort - bytes

playbooks.name: GitHub Actions script injection via pull request title or branch name
playbooks.summary: Use when a workflow interpolates untrusted event fields such as a PR title, issue body, or branch name into a run step, and an attacker crafts that field to execute commands on the runner.

preparation: Lint workflows for direct use of github.event fields inside run blocks
Set default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions to read for all repositories
Retain workflow run logs long enough to review historical runs
identification: Find the PR or issue whose title or branch name contained shell metacharacters
Review the workflow run log for the injected command output
Determine which secrets and token permissions the triggered workflow had
Search other repositories for the same vulnerable workflow pattern
containment: Disable the vulnerable workflow in the repository
Rotate secrets available to the workflow run
Close the malicious PR and block the submitting account from the organisation
eradication: Rewrite the workflow to pass untrusted values through environment variables
Revert commits, tags, or releases made with the run's GITHUB_TOKEN
Delete caches the injected job could have poisoned
recovery: Re-enable the fixed workflow and run it on a benign test PR
Verify release artifacts were not produced from the injected run
Notify maintainers of other repositories using the same template
lessons: Add a workflow static analysis check to required status checks
Review use of pull_request_target and issue_comment triggers organisation-wide
Track how many workflows had write-scoped tokens by default

splunk.title: Workflow runs triggered by external PRs
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action="workflows.created_workflow_run" repo="<org>/<repo>" | table _time actor event head_branch workflow_run_id

splunk.title: Writes by GITHUB_TOKEN during the run
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit actor="github-actions[bot]" action IN ("git.push","release.create","protected_branch.update") repo="<org>/<repo>" | table _time action repo

playbooks.name: Persistence planted on a self-hosted GitHub runner
playbooks.summary: Use when a job on a self-hosted runner, often from a public repository or fork, left a background process, cron job, or modified runner binary that survives across later jobs.

preparation: Never attach self-hosted runners to public repositories
Configure runners as ephemeral with just-in-time registration
Collect runner host auditd or EDR telemetry centrally
identification: List processes still running on the runner that started during a past job
Check crontab, systemd units, and shell profiles on the runner for new entries
Verify the runner agent binary hash against the official release
Identify the job and repository that introduced the persistence
containment: Remove the runner registration from the organisation
Network-isolate the runner host
Rotate secrets and tokens used by jobs that ran after the persistence appeared
eradication: Rebuild the runner from a fresh image instead of cleaning it
Restrict the runner group to specific private repositories
Remove the runner registration token from any location it was stored
recovery: Register the new runner as ephemeral and confirm it deregisters after each job
Rebuild artifacts produced on the runner after the persistence date
Monitor the new runner for long-lived processes between jobs
lessons: Add an alert for processes on runners that outlive their job
Audit runner group repository access across the organisation
Review fork PR approval requirements for workflows on self-hosted runners

splunk.title: Runner registration and group changes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action IN ("org.register_self_hosted_runner","org.remove_self_hosted_runner","org.runner_group_updated","repo.register_self_hosted_runner") | table _time actor action repo runner_name

splunk.title: Cron and systemd persistence on runner
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.dest="<runner_host>" Processes.process_name IN ("crontab","systemctl","nohup","setsid") by Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.user

playbooks.name: Build pipeline definition tampered to inject a backdoor
playbooks.summary: Use when a pipeline file such as a Jenkinsfile, workflow, or .gitlab-ci.yml is modified to download extra code, patch sources during build, or publish a modified artifact without a matching source change.

preparation: Require code owner review for changes to pipeline definition files
Produce provenance attestations linking each artifact to its source commit and pipeline
Keep pipeline definitions in protected branches only
identification: Diff pipeline definitions against the last reviewed version to find the inserted steps
Identify who committed the change and whether it bypassed review
List artifacts built by the tampered pipeline and where they were deployed
Rebuild one artifact from clean definitions and compare hashes with the released one
containment: Revert the pipeline definition and lock the branch
Stop deployments of artifacts produced after the tamper
Suspend the committing account pending investigation
eradication: Remove tampered artifacts from registries and release pages
Rotate secrets the tampered steps had access to
Check for the same insertion in other repositories using shared templates
recovery: Rebuild and redeploy clean artifacts with provenance verification
Notify customers if tampered builds were distributed externally
Verify deployment gates check provenance before release
lessons: Add a detection for pipeline file changes merged without code owner approval
Review how the committer obtained write access
Adopt reproducible builds for release artifacts

splunk.title: Commits touching pipeline definition files
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action="git.push" repo="<org>/<repo>" | search "Jenkinsfile" OR ".github/workflows" OR ".gitlab-ci.yml" | table _time actor repo ref

splunk.title: Merges that bypassed required reviews
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action IN ("protected_branch.policy_override","protected_branch.rejected_ref_update","pull_request.merge") repo="<org>/<repo>" | table _time actor action branch

splunk.title: Jenkins job config changes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=jenkins* ("config.xml" OR "Configuration changed" OR "job/<job_name>") | table _time user message

playbooks.name: Artifact repository (Artifactory or Nexus) poisoned with tampered packages
playbooks.summary: Use when an internal artifact repository serves packages or binaries that differ from what CI published, for example after an attacker overwrote a release or added a higher-version internal package.

preparation: Disable artifact overwrite on release repositories
Record checksums of every artifact at publish time in an independent store
Ship repository access and audit logs to the SIEM
identification: Compare stored checksums with current artifact checksums across release repositories
Review repository audit logs for deploy or delete events by non-CI users
Identify consumers that downloaded the tampered artifact versions
Check for dependency confusion: new internal-named packages proxied from public registries
containment: Remove or quarantine tampered artifacts and block their versions
Revoke the repository credentials or tokens used for the unauthorised deploys
Freeze deploy permissions to release repositories except for the CI service account
eradication: Republish clean artifacts from verified CI builds
Purge tampered versions from downstream caches and build agents
Add namespace exclusion rules so internal package names never resolve from remotes
recovery: Redeploy services that consumed tampered artifacts
Re-verify all release artifacts against provenance before re-enabling consumers
Patch the repository server if a vulnerability allowed the deploy
lessons: Add alerting on artifact deploys by any user other than CI
Review token scope given to developers on release repositories
Enable signature verification on artifact consumption

splunk.title: Artifact deploys and deletes by user
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=artifactory:access (action=ACCEPTED_DEPLOY OR action=ACCEPTED_DELETE) repo="<release_repo>" | stats count values(path) as paths by user ip | sort - count

splunk.title: Downloads of tampered artifact versions
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=artifactory:request request_url="*<artifact_path>/<version>*" | stats count by remote_address username | sort - count

playbooks.name: Developer laptop compromised with SSH keys and Git credentials
playbooks.summary: Use when malware or an intruder is found on a developer's machine holding SSH private keys, Git tokens, and cloud CLI credentials that reach source code and production servers.

preparation: Store developer SSH keys on hardware tokens or in an agent that requires touch
Issue short-lived SSH certificates instead of static authorised keys
Inventory which servers trust each developer's public key
identification: Determine what malware ran and when, using EDR timeline on the laptop
List private keys, Git tokens, and cloud CLI profiles present in the user's home directory
Search SSH logs on servers for logins with the developer's key from unknown sources
Review Git hosting audit logs for pushes and clones by the developer's identity
containment: Isolate the laptop through EDR
Remove the developer's public keys from Git hosting and server authorised_keys
Revoke the developer's Git tokens and cloud CLI sessions
eradication: Reimage the laptop
Review commits pushed during the compromise window for malicious changes
Remove any additional keys the attacker added to servers or Git accounts
recovery: Issue new hardware-backed keys to the developer
Restore developer access step by step with fresh credentials
Monitor the developer's identities for anomalies for 30 days
lessons: Measure how many servers trusted a single static developer key
Move server access to SSH certificates with short validity
Review EDR coverage gaps on developer machines

splunk.title: SSH logins with the developer's account
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=linux_secure "Accepted publickey" user="<dev_user>" | stats count values(host) as hosts by src | sort - count

splunk.title: Git keys added to the developer's account
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action IN ("public_key.create","oauth_access.create","personal_access_token.request_created") actor="<dev_user>" | table _time action actor_ip

playbooks.name: Terraform state file exposed with embedded secrets
playbooks.summary: Use when a Terraform state file, which stores resource attributes and often plaintext passwords and keys, is found in a public bucket, artifact, or repository.

preparation: Store state in a private encrypted backend with access logging
Mark sensitive outputs and avoid writing secrets into resource attributes
Block public access at the account level for state buckets
identification: Locate every copy of the exposed state file and its exposure start time
Parse the state to list database passwords, keys, and tokens it contains
Check bucket access logs for downloads of the state file by unknown principals
Map the infrastructure described in the state to judge attack surface revealed
containment: Remove public access and delete exposed copies of the state
Rotate every secret value found in the state file
Lock the backend to the CI role and named administrators
eradication: Refactor modules so secrets come from a secrets manager at runtime
Run terraform apply with rotated values and confirm state no longer holds old secrets
Check cloud logs for activity using the exposed credentials
recovery: Verify infrastructure drift is zero after re-applying
Re-enable pipelines that use the state backend
Confirm bucket policies deny public reads
lessons: Add scanning for .tfstate files in repositories and artifacts
Count secrets that were stored in state versus fetched at runtime
Review how the state copy ended up outside the backend

splunk.title: Reads of state objects in the backend bucket
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=s3.amazonaws.com eventName=GetObject requestParameters.bucketName="<state_bucket>" | stats count by userIdentity.arn sourceIPAddress requestParameters.key

splunk.title: Public access changes on the state bucket
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventName IN ("PutBucketPolicy","PutBucketAcl","DeletePublicAccessBlock") requestParameters.bucketName="<state_bucket>" | table _time userIdentity.arn eventName sourceIPAddress

playbooks.name: Code-signing key or passphrase exposed in build logs
playbooks.summary: Use when CI job output reveals a signing key, keystore password, or GPG passphrase, for example through a debug flag or echo, and the logs are visible to many users or retained externally.

preparation: Keep signing keys in an HSM or signing service so CI never handles key material
Enable secret masking for all signing-related variables
Know who can view job logs in each CI project
identification: Identify the job runs and log lines that exposed the key material
List users and integrations that viewed or downloaded the logs
Check whether logs were forwarded to external log stores
Search for artifacts signed with the key outside the release pipeline
containment: Delete or redact the affected job logs in CI and log stores
Revoke the signing key or certificate and generate a replacement
Remove the debug setting that caused the output
eradication: Move signing to a service that signs hashes without exposing the key
Re-sign current releases with the new key
Remove the old key from all CI variables and backups
recovery: Publish the new signing key fingerprint to consumers
Update update-verification pins in clients that check the signature
Verify new builds sign successfully through the new path
lessons: Add log scanning for private key headers in CI output
Review why masking did not catch the value
Limit job log visibility to project maintainers

splunk.title: Private key material in collected CI logs
splunk.spl: index=* (sourcetype=jenkins* OR sourcetype=gitlab:job OR sourcetype=github:actions:log) ("BEGIN PRIVATE KEY" OR "BEGIN PGP PRIVATE" OR "storepass") | stats count by sourcetype source host

splunk.title: Log downloads for affected runs
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action="workflows.download_workflow_run_logs" OR action="workflows.delete_workflow_run_logs" repo="<org>/<repo>" | table _time actor actor_ip action

playbooks.name: npm or PyPI publishing token leaked
playbooks.summary: Use when a token that can publish your organisation's packages to npm or PyPI is exposed, so an attacker could push a malicious version that your customers install automatically.

preparation: Use trusted publishing via OIDC instead of long-lived registry tokens
Require 2FA for all maintainers of organisation packages
List all packages each token can publish
identification: Identify the token's scope and the packages it can publish
Review the registry's publish history for versions not produced by CI
Diff any unexpected version against the tagged source
Check download counts of any unexpected version since publication
containment: Revoke the token in the registry account settings
Deprecate or yank unauthorised versions and contact registry security for removal
Reset passwords and 2FA for maintainer accounts linked to the token
eradication: Remove the leaked token from CI variables, dotfiles, and wherever it was exposed
Republish a clean higher version so consumers upgrade off the malicious one
Audit package collaborators and remove unknown ones
recovery: Publish an advisory with affected versions and indicators for consumers
Move publishing to trusted publishing with provenance attestation
Monitor the registry for new versions not from your CI
lessons: Add alerting on registry publish events not tied to a CI run
Review how the token leaked and add scanning for registry token formats
Measure time between unauthorised publish and yank

splunk.title: Leaked token pattern in repos or logs
splunk.spl: index=* ("npm_" OR "pypi-AgEI") NOT sourcetype=github:audit | regex _raw="(npm_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}|pypi-AgEI[A-Za-z0-9_-]{50,})" | stats count by sourcetype source host

splunk.title: Publish workflow runs in CI
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action="workflows.completed_workflow_run" workflow_name="*publish*" | table _time repo actor head_sha conclusion

playbooks.name: Repository deploy key abused for unauthorised access
playbooks.summary: Use when a deploy key attached to a repository, often with write access and no owner, is used from an unknown host to clone code or push commits.

preparation: Inventory deploy keys per repository with owner, purpose, and read or write flag
Prefer read-only deploy keys or GitHub Apps for automation
Capture git clone and push audit events with source IP
identification: Identify the deploy key fingerprint and which repository it belongs to
List clones and pushes using that key with source IPs
Find the system where the private key is supposed to live
Review pushed commits for malicious changes if the key had write access
containment: Delete the deploy key from the repository
Block the source IPs seen using the key
Revert unauthorised commits and protect affected branches
eradication: Remove the private key from the host it leaked from and check that host for compromise
Search other repositories for the same public key reused as a deploy key
Replace the automation's access with a scoped GitHub App
recovery: Issue a new read-only key or app installation to the automation
Verify the automation works with reduced access
Watch the repository for further clones from unknown IPs
lessons: Audit and remove stale deploy keys organisation-wide
Alert on deploy key use from IPs outside known automation hosts
Review why the key had write permission

splunk.title: Git operations by deploy key
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action IN ("git.clone","git.push","git.fetch") programmatic_access_type="Deploy key" repo="<org>/<repo>" | stats count by actor_ip action | sort - count

splunk.title: Deploy key lifecycle events
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action IN ("repo.add_deploy_key","repo.remove_deploy_key","deploy_key.create","deploy_key.destroy") | table _time actor repo action fingerprint

playbooks.name: Branch protection disabled and history force-pushed
playbooks.summary: Use when protection rules on a main or release branch are switched off and a force-push rewrites history, possibly hiding malicious commits or destroying legitimate work.

preparation: Restrict who can modify branch protection or rulesets to organisation owners
Mirror critical repositories to a read-only backup that keeps all refs
Alert on branch protection and ruleset changes in the audit log
identification: Identify who disabled the protection rule and from which IP
Recover the pre-force-push SHA from the audit log, reflog, or backup mirror
Diff old and new histories to find removed and added commits
Confirm whether the actor's account or token was compromised
containment: Re-enable branch protection and rulesets on the affected branch
Suspend the actor's access or revoke the token used
Halt deployments from the affected branch
eradication: Restore the branch to the verified pre-incident SHA
Remove malicious commits introduced in the rewritten history
Check other repositories for protection changes by the same actor
recovery: Ask developers to rebase local work onto the restored history
Redeploy from the restored branch once reviewed
Confirm CI and release tags point to legitimate commits
lessons: Measure how long protection was disabled
Move to organisation-level rulesets that repository admins cannot bypass
Review admin role assignments that allowed the change

splunk.title: Branch protection and ruleset changes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action IN ("protected_branch.destroy","protected_branch.update","repository_ruleset.update","repository_ruleset.destroy") | table _time actor actor_ip repo branch action

splunk.title: Force pushes on protected branches
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action="git.push" repo="<org>/<repo>" | search forced=true OR "force" | table _time actor actor_ip ref before after

playbooks.name: Malicious VS Code extension installed by developers
playbooks.summary: Use when a Visual Studio Code extension from the marketplace or a VSIX file is found exfiltrating files, tokens, or keystrokes from developer machines.

preparation: Configure an extension allowlist through VS Code enterprise policy
Collect installed IDE extensions from developer endpoints into the inventory
Monitor node processes spawned by the IDE in EDR
identification: Find all endpoints with the extension ID and version installed
Analyse the extension package for network calls and file paths it reads
Search proxy logs for the extension's exfiltration domain
List secrets present in workspaces opened on affected machines
containment: Uninstall the extension remotely and block its ID in policy
Block the exfiltration domain at the proxy
Revoke Git, cloud, and registry tokens on affected developer machines
eradication: Delete the extension folder from user profiles on every endpoint
Check for persistence the extension set up outside the IDE
Report the extension to the marketplace for takedown
recovery: Reissue developer credentials after cleanup is confirmed
Provide an approved alternative extension if one is needed
Re-scan the inventory to confirm zero installs remain
lessons: Measure installs before detection and how they were sourced
Add detection for IDE child processes making external connections
Educate developers on publisher verification in the marketplace

splunk.title: IDE-spawned processes on developer hosts
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("Code.exe","code","Code Helper*") Processes.process_name IN ("curl","powershell.exe","cmd.exe","sh") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process

splunk.title: Traffic to extension exfiltration domain
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.dest IN ("<ioc_domain>") by Web.src Web.user Web.http_method | sort - count

playbooks.name: Leaked .npmrc or .pypirc file with registry credentials
playbooks.summary: Use when a package manager config file containing auth tokens for public or private registries is committed, baked into an image, or shared, exposing read or publish access.

preparation: Add .npmrc and .pypirc to global gitignore templates and secret scanning rules
Use environment variable references in registry configs rather than literal tokens
Know which registries issue tokens to developers and CI
identification: Extract the registry URLs and token identifiers from the leaked file
Determine whether each token has read-only or publish rights
Find where the file was exposed: repository, image layer, ticket, or chat
Review registry logs for use of the token from unfamiliar IPs
containment: Revoke every token found in the file at its registry
Delete or redact the exposed file at its location
Check the private registry for packages downloaded with the token
eradication: Issue replacement tokens scoped read-only where possible
Update CI and developer configs to read tokens from environment or a credential helper
Scan other repositories and images for the same config pattern
recovery: Confirm builds authenticate with the new tokens
Verify no unexpected versions were published with the old token
Notify the token owner of the new configuration approach
lessons: Add .npmrc and .pypirc literal-token detection to CI checks
Review whether developers need publish rights at all
Track the number of registry tokens per developer

splunk.title: Registry token use from unfamiliar IPs
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=artifactory:request username="<token_user>" | stats count values(request_url) as urls by remote_address | sort - count

splunk.title: Config files in recent pushes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit action IN ("secret_scanning_alert.create","secret_scanning_alert.reopen") secret_type IN ("npm_access_token","pypi_api_token") | table _time repo secret_type

playbooks.name: Cloud credentials found in Docker image layers
playbooks.summary: Use when a container image pushed to a registry contains cloud access keys or service account files in an intermediate layer, even if a later layer deleted them.

preparation: Scan every layer of images for secrets in CI before push
Use build secrets mounts instead of COPY or ARG for credentials
Know which registries are public and who can pull from private ones
identification: Inspect image history to find the layer and Dockerfile line that added the credentials
Determine whether the repository in the registry is public and its pull counts
List every tag and digest that contains the affected layer
Search cloud audit logs for use of the credentials outside your network
containment: Deactivate the access key or delete the service account key
Make the image repository private or delete affected tags
Block IPs that used the credentials
eradication: Rewrite the Dockerfile to use build secret mounts and rebuild the image
Delete all digests containing the secret layer from registries and mirrors
Reverse resources or IAM changes made with the credentials
recovery: Redeploy workloads using the rebuilt image
Switch workloads to workload identity instead of static keys
Confirm layer scanning passes on the new image
lessons: Add a CI gate that fails builds when any layer contains credentials
Measure pulls of the leaking image from outside the organisation
Review Dockerfile templates for ARG-based secret patterns

splunk.title: Activity by the leaked key outside your network
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.accessKeyId="<leaked_key_id>" NOT sourceIPAddress IN (<corp_egress_ips>) | stats count values(eventName) as events by sourceIPAddress awsRegion | sort - count

splunk.title: Pulls of the affected image repository
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=ecr.amazonaws.com eventName IN ("BatchGetImage","GetDownloadUrlForLayer") requestParameters.repositoryName="<repo>" | stats count by userIdentity.arn sourceIPAddress

playbooks.name: CI secrets exfiltrated through a pull request from a fork
playbooks.summary: Use when a contributor opens a PR from a fork that modifies build scripts or tests to print or send out secrets, and a pull_request_target or misconfigured pipeline ran it with secrets.

preparation: Require approval before running workflows for first-time and fork contributors
Avoid checking out PR head code in pull_request_target workflows
Separate secrets for release jobs from test jobs
identification: Review the fork PR diff for changes to build scripts, test hooks, or package scripts
Read the run logs for encoded output or outbound requests made during tests
List secrets exposed to the run via environment and the token's permissions
Identify other PRs from the same fork owner across the organisation
containment: Close the PR and block the user from the organisation
Rotate all secrets available to the triggered workflow
Change fork PR workflow approval to require approval for all outside collaborators
eradication: Refactor the workflow so untrusted code runs without secrets
Delete caches written by the fork run
Check cloud and registry logs for use of the exposed secrets
recovery: Re-run legitimate PR checks under the safer workflow
Confirm rotated secrets are distributed to remaining jobs
Inform the project maintainers of the new contribution process
lessons: Inventory workflows using pull_request_target with checkout of head ref
Add detection for fork-triggered runs that access secrets
Measure time between the run and secret rotation

splunk.title: Workflow runs from fork PRs

playbooks.name: Jenkins credential store dumped by an attacker
playbooks.summary: Use when Jenkins stored credentials are extracted, for example through the script console, a vulnerable plugin, or access to credentials.xml with its master key, exposing every system Jenkins deploys to.

preparation: Restrict script console and administer permission to a small named group
Keep Jenkins and plugins patched and track plugin versions centrally
Forward Jenkins audit trail and access logs to the SIEM
identification: Review audit trail for script console use and credentials plugin API calls
Check whether credentials.xml, secrets/master.key, and hudson.util.Secret were read on disk
List every credential ID in the store and the systems it reaches
Identify the entry point, such as an unpatched plugin or stolen admin session
containment: Restrict Jenkins network access to administrators only
Rotate all credentials in the store, starting with cloud and production deploy keys
Disable compromised Jenkins user accounts and API tokens
eradication: Patch the exploited plugin or core vulnerability
Remove malicious jobs, Groovy init scripts, or plugins added by the attacker
Regenerate the Jenkins master key and re-enter rotated credentials
recovery: Restore builds gradually, verifying job configs against version control
Review downstream systems for access using the old credentials
Move high-value secrets to an external vault fetched at runtime
lessons: Add an alert for script console usage
Measure count of credentials stored in Jenkins versus external vault
Review plugin patch latency

splunk.title: Jenkins script console and credential access
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=jenkins* ("/script" OR "/scriptText" OR "credentials-store" OR "/credentials/") | stats count values(uri) as uris by user src | sort - count

splunk.title: File reads of Jenkins secrets on the controller
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.dest="<jenkins_host>" Processes.process IN ("*credentials.xml*","*master.key*","*hudson.util.Secret*") by Processes.user Processes.process

splunk.title: Use of rotated deploy credentials after dump
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.user IN (<jenkins_cred_users>) by Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.action

playbooks.name: GitLab personal access token abused
playbooks.summary: Use when a GitLab personal access token is used from an unknown location to clone projects, read CI variables, or create new tokens and SSH keys for persistence.

preparation: Enforce PAT expiry limits and restrict scopes allowed for personal tokens
Stream GitLab audit events to the SIEM
Know how to revoke tokens via admin API in bulk
identification: Identify the token's owner, scopes, and creation date
List API calls and project exports made with the token from unknown IPs
Check for CI variable reads, which expose further secrets
Look for new PATs, SSH keys, or deploy tokens created by the owner's account
containment: Revoke the PAT and all other tokens for the owner
Block the source IPs at the GitLab ingress
Rotate CI variables in projects the token could read
eradication: Remove SSH keys, tokens, and webhooks the attacker created
Check affected projects for commits or pipeline changes made via the token
Investigate how the owner's token leaked
recovery: Issue a new scoped token with short expiry to the owner
Confirm integrations relying on the token use project access tokens instead
Monitor the owner's account for unusual API use
lessons: Measure tokens without expiry across the instance
Add an alert for project export requests from new IPs
Review whether the token needed api scope

splunk.title: Token activity from new IPs
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=gitlab:audit author_name="<user>" | stats count values(entity_path) as projects values(custom_message) as events by ip_address | sort - count

splunk.title: Token and key creation events
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=gitlab:audit ("personal access token" OR "SSH key" OR "deploy token") ("created" OR "added") | table _time author_name ip_address custom_message

playbooks.name: Slack webhook or API secret embedded in a mobile app binary
playbooks.summary: Use when a published iOS or Android app is found to contain a webhook URL, API key, or backend secret that anyone can extract by decompiling the app.

preparation: Scan compiled mobile builds for secrets before store submission
Route mobile API calls through a backend that holds secrets server-side
Know the app store expedited review process for urgent releases
identification: Decompile the released app version and confirm which secrets are present
Determine which app versions in the wild contain the secret
Review the target service's logs for use of the secret from non-app clients
Check the Slack channel for spam or phishing posts made through the webhook
containment: Regenerate the Slack webhook or revoke the API key
Delete spam or malicious messages posted through the webhook
Apply rate limits or IP restrictions on the backend API key if it cannot be rotated yet
eradication: Move the secret behind a backend proxy that authenticates the app user
Ship a new app version without embedded secrets
Force-upgrade old versions that would break after rotation
recovery: Verify the new app version functions with the backend proxy
Monitor the old secret's endpoint for continued attempts
Alert Slack workspace users to ignore messages from the old webhook
lessons: Add binary secret scanning to the mobile release pipeline
Track time from report to app store release
Review other apps built from the same template

splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_query="*<api_key_prefix>*" by Web.src Web.http_user_agent | sort - count

splunk.title: Slack webhook posting activity
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=slack:audit (action="app_installed" OR action="incoming_webhook*" OR entity.app.name="<webhook_app>") | table _time actor.user.email action context.location.name
